The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $y$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\frac{5}{7},$ what is the value of $sec⁡\theta ?$
worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/17e6320115f2cf8b5ffad6abc099169774536af20d2559b453aaa97c1286d96d.png)

We're given that $y=\frac{5}{7}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, $sin⁡\theta =\frac{5}{7}.$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $cos⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{5}{7}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{5}{7})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{25}{49}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{24}{49}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{24}}{7} \\  & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{6}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $cos⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =-\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{7}.$

Finally, knowing that $sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(-\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{7})}=-\frac{7}{2\sqrt{6}}=-\frac{7\sqrt{6}}{12}.
$$
